newsitem.title: ALGERIA: FEATURE - Forgotten war simmers in Sahara desert.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Forgotten war simmers in Sahara desert.

text.p: Deadly mines spelling out the letters R.A.S.D. shimmer under the relentless desert sun, relics of a war over the Western Sahara that threatens to rekindle after six years of ceasefire.

The mines, paying eerie homage to the self-proclaimed Arab Sahara Democratic Republic (RASD) whose Polisario Front fought a 15-year-long war against Morocco, are displayed in a bizarre military museum set up in the middle of a desert wasteland in southwest Algeria.

Tanks, armoured personnel carriers and jeeps are parked on sand inside an adobe-walled courtyard where the desert air has preserved them along with automatic weapons, mortars and the remains of a plane, the Moroccan flag still visible on its wing.

Photographs of dead soldiers and the family pictures they carried are also on display, grim reminders that the Polisario Front, which took up arms in 1976, were effective fighters against Morocco's larger and better-equipped army.
"We have captured all these things from Morocco in the war. This is to show our force, our ability to fight against a bigger power," the Polisario museum curator said.
"We can do it again, if necessary."

His warning was echoed by many other Saharwis who spoke to Reuters during a three-day tour of Hamada, a bleak, unforgiving stretch of the Sahara that houses the Polisario's base in Tindouf and its sprawling refugee camps.
There are some 170,000 refugees, according to the Polisario, who fled their homeland in the mid-1970s as Moroccans moved into the former Spanish colony.

They have tolerated the harsh conditions of the Hamada, known as "the desert of deserts", living in isolation in primitive huts and tents with disease-laden water supplies and limited food for more than 20 years.

They are ready to go home -- to a land rich in phosphates and with miles of Atlantic coast -- but insist "home" must be in an independent Western Sahara. Many say they are prepared to die fighting rather than live under Moroccan control.
REFUGEES READY TO FIGHT AGAIN

"We are ready to return to war if the Moroccans don't leave our country," Abdurah Aman, a squad leader fighting since 1975, said. "If we are here to get independence and if we've lost our mothers, fathers and brothers, it's not for any other reason."

Other signs show the Polisario is growing restless with the 1991 ceasefire brokered by the U.N. but whose planned follow-up referendum, to give Saharwis the choice of independence or integration with Morocco, collapsed.

Polisario took its military hardware out of mothballs and mounted an impressive display last month with several thousand troops stretched across the desert backed by some 70 Russian tanks, personnel carriers and missile launchers.
"We are a real army as you can see, and we fought against Morocco, which had 10 times as many soldiers," Aman said.
The Polisario showed they still had the skills of their nomadic ancestors, navigating their vehicles at high speeds without map or compass to meet up in precise formation.
Surviving with tens of thousands of people to house, clothe and feed in one of the world's most inhospitable deserts is also testament to the Polisario's organisational skills.

But a closer inspection of their troops showed them gripping weathered Russian Kalashnikov rifles and wearing ill-fitting uniforms of various kinds. In places their ranks thinned out, with some soldiers bent with age and missing helmets or guns.
In addition, Algeria's backing if fighting renews is far from guaranteed as it tries to strengthen ties with Morocco through the Arab Maghreb Union, a North African trading bloc.

The Polisario insists it is ready to fight, the younger men in the camps having been sent to the front -- a sliver of Western Sahara territory along the border with Algeria and Mauritania that the Polisario controls -- to train from age 18.
NOT READY TO SUBMIT TO MOROCCO
"We may be outnumbered, but we would rather go back to war than to Moroccan control," the spokesman said.

The U.N. redoubled efforts recently to find a solution to the conflict, which although small-scale, threatens stability of a sensitive region at NATO's southern flank. Its peace- monitoring and refugee aid is also a drain on U.N. resources.

U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan appointed James Baker, former U.S. Secretary of State, as his personal envoy to try to find a way to secure peace. Baker has toured the region and expressed optimism of finding an acceptable solution because, he said, the people were weary of the status quo.
But a word with one prisoner shows war still simmers. "The Western Sahara belongs to Morocco, that's all there is to it. I have been here 11 years and I'm prepared to die here," he said.
So are the refugees.
"I'm sure one day I'll be free, even if that means we have war again," Hadisha Omar, a resident at a women's camp, said. "We left everything there so we have nothing left to lose."
